questions.stem: Which type of pathogen is an infectious, misfolded protein with no nucleic acid?
options: A prion
A virus
A protist
A fungus
questions.explanation: Prions are misfolded proteins that cause normal copies of the same protein to misfold, as in Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease. Viruses are also non-cellular, but they contain DNA or RNA.

questions.stem: What defines an infectious disease?
options: It is caused by an inherited allele passed from parents to children
It is caused by a poor diet that lacks essential vitamins and minerals
It is caused by the body's own cells dividing without normal control
It is caused by a pathogen that can pass from one host to another
questions.explanation: An infectious disease results from invasion by a pathogen that can be transmitted between hosts. Inherited, nutritional and cancerous diseases are non-infectious because they cannot spread from person to person.

questions.stem: Malaria is caused by Plasmodium, a single-celled eukaryote, and spreads when an infected mosquito bites a person. Which pair correctly classifies the pathogen and its mode of transmission?
options: A bacterium, transmitted by a vector
A protist, transmitted by direct contact
A virus, transmitted in contaminated water
A protist, transmitted by a vector
questions.explanation: Plasmodium is a protist, a eukaryote that is not a plant, animal or fungus. The mosquito carries it between hosts, so it is a vector. Bacteria are prokaryotes, so a single-celled eukaryote cannot be a bacterium.

questions.stem: Cholera spreads when people drink water contaminated with faeces from infected people. Which public health measure would most directly reduce its spread?
options: Spraying insecticide to reduce the number of mosquitoes in the area
Wearing gloves when handling the blood of infected patients
Isolating patients so they cannot cough near other people
Treating drinking water and separating sewage from water supplies
questions.explanation: Cholera is transmitted through contaminated water, so clean water and sanitation break the chain of transmission. Mosquito control targets vector-borne diseases, which cholera is not.

questions.stem: Athlete's foot is a fungal infection often picked up from wet floors in shared showers. Which mode of transmission does this show?
options: Transmission through contaminated food
Transfer of blood during a medical procedure
Indirect contact with a contaminated surface
Transmission through a biting insect vector
questions.explanation: The fungus is left on the floor by one person and picked up by another, so it passes by indirect contact with a contaminated surface. No vector or food is involved.

questions.stem: Hepatitis B virus is found in the blood and other body fluids of infected people. Which situation carries a risk of transmitting it?
options: Drinking from a public water supply that is chlorinated
Being bitten by an insect that has not fed on a person
Sharing a needle that has been used by an infected person
Shaking hands with an infected person who has washed their hands
questions.explanation: Viruses carried in blood and body fluids spread when those fluids enter another person, as through a shared needle. Casual skin contact and treated water do not transfer blood.

questions.stem: Many viruses that cause colds trigger sneezing and a runny nose in their host. How does this help the virus?
options: It lowers the host's body temperature so the virus can replicate more quickly
It releases virus particles into the air and onto surfaces, helping transmission to new hosts
It moves virus particles deeper into the lungs, where there are more cells to infect
It removes antibodies from the nose so the virus can enter cells more easily
questions.explanation: Symptoms that expel droplets carry virus particles to other people, so they aid transmission between hosts. Sneezing moves material out of the airways, not deeper into the lungs.

questions.stem: A virus can only enter cells that carry a particular protein on their plasma membrane. Which explanation best accounts for this?
options: The virus can only cross membranes that lack phospholipids, so it needs this protein instead
The protein is an antibody that carries the virus into the cell by phagocytosis
The host cell makes the virus inside its nucleus only when the protein is present
Proteins on the virus surface bind only to a specific receptor shape on the host cell
questions.explanation: Viral surface proteins have a shape complementary to a specific receptor on the host cell, so the virus attaches to, and enters, only cells with that receptor. Antibodies are made by B lymphocytes, not displayed by host cells as entry points.

questions.stem: Some disease-causing bacteria have a thick slimy capsule around the cell wall. How is this an adaptation that helps them cause disease?
options: It makes them harder for phagocytes to engulf and destroy
It lets them inject their DNA directly into host cells
It allows them to photosynthesise inside the host's body
It prevents the host from making any antibodies against it
questions.explanation: A capsule helps bacteria resist being engulfed by phagocytes, so they survive longer in the host. It does not stop antibody production, although it can slow the innate response.

questions.stem: When pathogens enter a host, which change most directly triggers an immune response?
options: Immune cells detect foreign antigens and chemicals released by damaged cells
The host's red blood cells change shape and block the infected capillaries
The host's body temperature drops, which signals the bone marrow
Glucose levels in the blood rise sharply and stimulate the white blood cells to divide
questions.explanation: Immune cells recognise antigens that are foreign to the body, and damaged tissue releases chemicals such as histamine that start inflammation. Fever is a later response, and it raises temperature rather than lowering it.

questions.stem: Which is part of the first line of defence?
options: Neutrophils that engulf bacteria in an infected cut
Antibodies produced by B lymphocytes and released into the blood
Cytotoxic T cells that destroy virus-infected cells
Acid in the stomach that kills many swallowed microbes
questions.explanation: The first line of defence is physical and chemical barriers that stop pathogens entering, such as skin, mucus and stomach acid. Neutrophils are part of the second line, and antibodies and T cells are the third.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly describes the second line of defence?
options: It is adaptive and specific, involving memory cells from earlier infections
It is innate and non-specific, involving cells, chemicals and inflammation
It is adaptive and specific, involving B and T lymphocytes
It is innate and non-specific, made up of skin and mucous membranes
questions.explanation: The second line acts on any pathogen that gets past the barriers, using phagocytes, chemicals and the inflammatory response. Skin and mucous membranes are the first line, and lymphocytes and memory cells belong to the third.

questions.stem: The airways are lined with cells that produce mucus and cells with cilia. How do these work together to defend the body?
options: Mucus digests microbes, and cilia carry the products into the blood
Cilia engulf microbes, and mucus delivers them to the lymphocytes
Mucus produces antibodies, and cilia present the antigens to helper T cells
Mucus traps particles and microbes, and cilia sweep it up to the throat
questions.explanation: Sticky mucus traps dust and microbes, and the beating cilia move it up and out of the airways to be swallowed or coughed out. This is a first-line physical barrier; cilia do not engulf cells.

questions.stem: Tears and saliva contain lysozyme. What is its role in defence?
options: It is an antibody that binds to one specific bacterial antigen
It is a hormone that raises body temperature during an infection
It is a chemical that attracts lymphocytes into the tear ducts
It is an enzyme that breaks down the cell walls of some bacteria
questions.explanation: Lysozyme is an enzyme that damages bacterial cell walls, a non-specific chemical barrier. Antibodies are specific proteins made in the third line of defence.

questions.stem: A splinter carries bacteria into the skin, and within hours the area is red, swollen, warm and painful. Which event causes the redness and warmth?
options: Cytotoxic T cells release heat as they destroy body cells near the splinter
Histamine dilates nearby blood vessels, increasing blood flow to the area
Antibodies bind to the bacteria and make them glow red under the skin
Red blood cells leave the capillaries and engulf the invading bacteria
questions.explanation: Damaged cells and mast cells release histamine, which dilates arterioles and makes capillaries leakier. More blood reaches the area, causing redness and warmth, and fluid leaking out causes swelling. Red blood cells do not engulf bacteria.

questions.stem: During inflammation, capillaries in the infected area become more permeable. How does this help fight the infection?
options: Memory cells can be released from the blood to stop the swelling quickly
Phagocytes and fluid with defensive proteins can move out into the tissue
Pathogens can leave the tissue and enter the blood to be filtered out
Red blood cells can carry extra oxygen directly to the pathogens
questions.explanation: Leakier capillary walls let phagocytes such as neutrophils, and plasma containing defensive proteins, reach the infected tissue. Spreading pathogens into the blood would make the infection worse, not better.

questions.stem: What is the role of mast cells in the inflammatory response?
options: They kill body cells that have been infected by viruses
They release histamine, which starts inflammation
They produce antibodies against a specific antigen
They engulf and digest most of the invading bacteria
questions.explanation: Mast cells in tissues release histamine when tissue is damaged or infected, triggering vasodilation and leaky capillaries. Antibodies come from B lymphocytes, and killing infected cells is done by cytotoxic T cells.

questions.stem: Which type of white blood cell is usually the first phagocyte to arrive in large numbers at a site of infection?
options: Mast cell
Helper T cell
Neutrophil
B lymphocyte
questions.explanation: Neutrophils are the most abundant white blood cells and move quickly from the blood into infected tissue to engulf pathogens. Mast cells release histamine but are not the main phagocytes, and lymphocytes belong to the adaptive response.

questions.stem: Which sequence correctly describes phagocytosis of a bacterium by a macrophage?
options: The membrane releases antibodies, which digest the bacterium outside the cell
The bacterium is pumped in by a carrier protein, then the nucleus digests it
The membrane surrounds the bacterium, forms a vesicle, and lysosomes add digestive enzymes
The bacterium diffuses through the membrane, then ribosomes add digestive enzymes
questions.explanation: Phagocytosis is a form of endocytosis: the plasma membrane extends around the particle and pinches off to form a vesicle. Lysosomes fuse with it and their enzymes digest the bacterium. A whole bacterium is far too large to diffuse or be carried through the membrane.

questions.stem: A person has a fever during an infection. Why is a moderate fever thought to be part of the body's defence?
options: It makes the skin more acidic so that pathogens cannot enter the body
It slows the replication of many pathogens and speeds up some immune reactions
It denatures the pathogens' proteins without affecting any of the body's proteins
It produces memory cells that give long-term immunity to the pathogen
questions.explanation: A raised body temperature slows the growth of many pathogens adapted to 37 degrees and can speed up immune reactions. It is not selective enough to denature only pathogen proteins, which is why very high fevers are dangerous.

questions.stem: What is an antigen?
options: A protein made by B lymphocytes that binds to a specific foreign molecule
A chemical released by mast cells that dilates nearby blood vessels
A phagocytic cell that engulfs pathogens and presents their fragments
A molecule that the immune system recognises and that triggers a specific response
questions.explanation: An antigen is any molecule, usually a protein or carbohydrate, that the immune system recognises and responds to. The protein made by B lymphocytes that binds an antigen is an antibody.

questions.stem: How do antigen-presenting cells such as dendritic cells and macrophages link the innate and adaptive responses?
options: They kill virus-infected cells and then become memory cells for that virus
They engulf pathogens and display the pathogen's antigens to T lymphocytes
They produce antibodies that coat pathogens before phagocytes arrive
They release histamine so that lymphocytes can leave the blood vessels
questions.explanation: Antigen-presenting cells engulf pathogens, break them down and display fragments of their antigens on their surface. Helper T cells with matching receptors are activated, starting the adaptive response.

questions.stem: Which cells provide humoral immunity?
options: B lymphocytes, which produce antibodies
Cytotoxic T cells, which kill infected cells
Neutrophils, which engulf bacteria
Mast cells, which release histamine
questions.explanation: Humoral immunity is antibody-mediated: B lymphocytes, once activated, multiply and produce antibodies that circulate in body fluids. Cytotoxic T cells provide cell-mediated immunity.

questions.stem: During an adaptive immune response, what do helper T cells do?
options: They release histamine to make capillaries leakier so lymphocytes can reach tissue
They bind directly to free antigens in the blood and neutralise them like antibodies
They recognise presented antigen and release chemicals that activate B cells and cytotoxic T cells
They engulf pathogens at the site of infection and digest them using lysosomes
questions.explanation: Helper T cells are activated by antigen-presenting cells and release signalling chemicals (cytokines) that stimulate matching B cells and cytotoxic T cells to multiply. They coordinate the response rather than destroying pathogens themselves.

questions.stem: A virus has entered a person's body cells and is replicating inside them. Which response directly destroys these infected cells?
options: Mast cells release histamine that bursts the infected cells
Memory B cells engulf the infected cells by phagocytosis
Cytotoxic T cells recognise and kill the infected body cells
Antibodies enter the infected cells and digest the virus inside
questions.explanation: Viruses inside cells are hidden from antibodies, so cell-mediated immunity is needed: cytotoxic T cells recognise antigens displayed by infected cells and kill them. Antibodies act outside cells.

questions.stem: A disease destroys most of a person's helper T cells. Why does this weaken both humoral and cell-mediated immunity?
options: Helper T cells are the only cells that can make antibodies against viruses
Helper T cells form the skin barrier that keeps pathogens out of the body
Helper T cells are the main phagocytes that engulf both bacteria and viruses
Helper T cells are needed to activate both B cells and cytotoxic T cells
questions.explanation: Without helper T cells, B cells and cytotoxic T cells are poorly activated, so both arms of adaptive immunity fail. HIV causes this by infecting helper T cells. Antibodies are made by B lymphocytes, not helper T cells.

questions.stem: What is the role of regulatory T cells?
options: They produce antibodies that remain in the blood after an infection
They engulf antigens and present them to other lymphocytes
They release histamine at the start of an inflammatory response
They suppress the immune response once an infection is controlled
questions.explanation: Regulatory T cells damp down the immune response after the pathogen is cleared and help stop the immune system attacking the body's own cells. Antigen presentation is done by dendritic cells and macrophages.

questions.stem: How do antibodies help destroy bacteria in the blood?
options: They enter the bacteria and stop their ribosomes from making proteins
They engulf the bacteria and digest them with enzymes from lysosomes
They raise the blood's temperature until the bacteria are denatured
They bind to specific antigens, clumping the bacteria and marking them for phagocytes
questions.explanation: Each antibody binds a specific antigen; with two or more binding sites it can link pathogens into clumps and neutralise them, and bound antibodies mark pathogens for phagocytes. Antibodies are proteins, not cells, so they cannot engulf anything.

questions.stem: Only a few of a person's millions of B lymphocytes respond to a newly invading bacterium. Why?
options: Only B cells that have previously been inside a phagocyte are able to make antibodies
Most B cells are found in the skin, where they form part of the first line of defence
Each B cell has receptors for one antigen, so only cells matching the bacterium's antigens are selected
Most B cells are destroyed by the bacterium, leaving only a few resistant cells to respond
questions.explanation: Each B lymphocyte carries receptors for one particular antigen. Only cells whose receptors match the invader's antigens are activated to multiply into antibody-producing cells and memory cells, so the response is specific.

questions.stem: A person is infected with the same strain of virus twice, two years apart. Compared with the first infection, the antibody response to the second is:
options: the same, because each infection is treated as entirely new
absent, because antibodies from the first infection are still present
faster and larger, because memory cells respond to the antigen
slower and smaller, because the virus has become resistant
questions.explanation: Memory B and T cells formed in the first response recognise the antigen quickly, so the secondary response is faster, larger and longer-lasting, often before symptoms appear. Antibodies from the first infection mostly decline within months.

questions.stem: A newborn baby has antibodies that crossed the placenta from its mother. What type of immunity is this?
options: Artificial active immunity
Natural passive immunity
Natural active immunity
Artificial passive immunity
questions.explanation: The baby received ready-made antibodies without its own immune system producing them, so the immunity is passive, and it arose naturally. It fades within months because no memory cells are made.

questions.stem: After a snake bite in the bush, a hiker is given antivenom, which contains antibodies against the venom. What type of immunity does this give?
options: Natural passive immunity, which lasts for the rest of the hiker's life
Natural active immunity, which produces memory cells against the venom
Artificial passive immunity, which is immediate but short-lived
Artificial active immunity, which is slow to start but long-lasting
questions.explanation: Injected antibodies act immediately, but the hiker's own lymphocytes did not make them and no memory cells form, so the protection is passive and temporary. Active immunity would take days or weeks to develop.

questions.stem: How does a vaccine give long-term protection against a disease?
options: It kills any pathogens already present in the body during infection
It strengthens the skin and mucous membranes against that pathogen
It exposes the immune system to the pathogen's antigens, producing memory cells
It supplies ready-made antibodies that stay in the blood for life
questions.explanation: A vaccine contains antigens from a killed, weakened or partial pathogen, or instructions to make them. The person's own adaptive response produces memory cells, which is artificial active immunity. Supplying ready-made antibodies gives passive immunity, which fades.

questions.stem: A booster dose of a vaccine is given several months after the first dose. Which outcome is the main purpose of the booster?
options: A stronger secondary response that increases antibody levels and memory cell numbers
A replacement of all the memory cells that the first dose destroyed
A switch from active immunity to passive immunity that lasts longer
A first-line barrier response that stops the pathogen entering the body
questions.explanation: The booster triggers a secondary response from the memory cells made after the first dose, giving higher antibody levels and more memory cells, so protection is stronger and longer-lasting. The first dose does not destroy memory cells.

questions.stem: What does the term herd immunity describe?
options: Protection that a person gains after recovering from several different infections
Indirect protection of unimmunised people when most of a population is immune
Immunity that a person inherits from both parents at the time of conception
Immunity passed from a mother to her baby through the placenta or milk
questions.explanation: When a high proportion of a population is immune, a pathogen rarely finds a susceptible host, so transmission chains break and unimmunised people are protected indirectly. Antibodies passed from mother to baby give passive immunity, not herd immunity.

questions.stem: Vaccination rates for a highly contagious disease fall in one town, while the neighbouring town keeps a high rate. Why is an outbreak more likely in the first town?
options: Unvaccinated people produce the pathogen spontaneously when the vaccination rate falls
The pathogen mutates only in towns where vaccination rates are low, making it much more deadly
More susceptible people allow each case to infect others, so chains of transmission continue
The vaccine becomes less effective in each person when fewer people in the town receive it
questions.explanation: With fewer immune people, an infected person is more likely to meet susceptible people, so each case can lead to further cases and an outbreak spreads. The vaccine works the same in each vaccinated person whatever the rate in the town.

questions.stem: During an outbreak of a respiratory disease, which combination of measures would most reduce its spread through a population?
options: Giving antibiotics to everyone, including healthy people with no symptoms
Encouraging travel between towns so that immunity spreads more evenly
Isolating cases, vaccinating contacts and limiting crowding in enclosed spaces
Treating drinking water, cooking food well and controlling mosquito numbers
questions.explanation: Respiratory pathogens spread by droplets between people, so isolation, vaccination and reducing crowding cut the number of new infections from each case. Water treatment and mosquito control target water-borne and vector-borne diseases, and antibiotics do not act on viruses.

questions.stem: In Australia, Ross River virus is spread to people by mosquitoes. Which action targets the vector rather than the pathogen?
options: Testing donated blood for the virus before it is used
Draining standing water where mosquitoes breed near homes
Developing an antiviral drug that stops the virus replicating
Giving patients antibodies against the virus after infection
questions.explanation: Mosquitoes are the vector, so removing their breeding sites reduces bites and transmission. Antiviral drugs and antibodies act on the virus itself, and blood testing targets a different route.
